meta.title: Atlas of Life
meta.method: Ages, authorities, species and formations from the Paleobiology Database; descriptive data paraphrased from the cited literature and English Wikipedia; images from Wikimedia Commons and PhyloPic with their licences.

clades.name: Anhangueria
clades.sum: Large, toothed, often crested fish-eating pterosaurs of the Early to early Late Cretaceous (ornithocheirids, anhanguerids and kin).
diag: Jaw tips expanded into a tooth rosette
Rounded crests on the snout and/or lower jaw in many species
Very long wings
clades.notes: The most diverse and successful pterosaurs of the Early Cretaceous; include some of the largest toothed pterosaurs (Tropeognathus, ~8.3 m).

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Ornithocheiromorpha”. English Wikipedia, revision 1369303086.

clades.name: Anurognathidae
clades.sum: Small, short-faced, short-tailed ‘frog-jawed’ pterosaurs of the Jurassic and Early Cretaceous of Europe and Asia.
diag: Skull wider than long, with a very broad gape
Large eyes
Short tail
Peg-like or slender recurved teeth
clades.notes: Wingspans up to about 90 cm. Usually seen as aerial insect-catchers. Their position in the pterosaur tree is disputed.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Anurognathidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1384401713.

clades.name: Azhdarchidae
clades.sum: Long-necked, toothless ‘terrestrial stalkers’ of the Late Cretaceous, including the largest flying animals known.
diag: Very long, stiff neck vertebrae
Long toothless beak
Long legs and small feet suited to walking
clades.notes: Sizes from cat-sized to 10–12 m wingspans (Quetzalcoatlus, Hatzegopteryx). The last pterosaurs before the end-Cretaceous extinction.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Azhdarchidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383713244.
Witton, M. P.; Naish, D. (2008). A reappraisal of azhdarchid pterosaur functional morphology and paleoecology. PLOS ONE 3(5): e2271. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0002271

clades.name: Azhdarchoidea
clades.sum: Toothless pterodactyloids with relatively short arms and long legs, good walkers — from tapejarids to giant azhdarchids.
diag: Low arm-to-leg length ratio
Toothless jaws
Many with large head crests
clades.notes: Defined by Unwin (2003) as Quetzalcoatlus + Tapejara and all descendants. Several genera (Alanqa, Xericeps, Leptostomia, Keresdrakon, Inabtanin) are placed here as incertae sedis.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Azhdarchoidea”. English Wikipedia, revision 1369335323.
Unwin, D. M. (2003). On the phylogeny and evolutionary history of pterosaurs. Geological Society, London, Special Publications 217: 139–190.

clades.name: Boreopteridae
clades.sum: Long-snouted pterodactyloids with needle-like teeth, from the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation of China.
diag: Long, low snout
Long, sharp needle-like teeth, longest at the front
clades.notes: Placed near ornithocheirids by its describers but near Cycnorhamphus (Gallodactylidae) by Andres & Myers (2013). Placed here directly under Pterodactyloidea.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Boreopteridae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383158392.

clades.name: Chaoyangopteridae
clades.sum: Toothless, mostly Early Cretaceous azhdarchoids, probably ground foragers like azhdarchids.
diag: Very large nasoantorbital fenestra reaching back to the braincase
Toothless jaws
Long neck and legs
clades.notes: Defined by Lü & Unwin (2008). Sometimes treated as a subfamily (Chaoyangopterinae) of Tapejaridae.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Chaoyangopteridae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383158453.

clades.name: Ctenochasmatidae
clades.sum: Filter- and sieve-feeding pterosaurs with combs of long, thin teeth, from the Late Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous.
diag: Long snouts packed with many slender, often outward-pointing teeth
Teeth forming a filtering comb or basket
clades.notes: Andres (2021) recognised three subfamilies: Ctenochasmatinae, Gnathosaurinae and Moganopterinae.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Ctenochasmatidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383158638.
Andres, B. (2021). Phylogenetic systematics of Quetzalcoatlus Lawson 1975 (Pterodactyloidea: Azhdarchoidea). Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology 41(sup1): 203–217.

clades.name: Ctenochasmatoidea
clades.sum: Early pterodactyloids — Pterodactylus, gallodactylids and ctenochasmatids — from the Late Jurassic to the late Early Cretaceous.
diag: Distinctive jaws and highly specialised teeth
Many species with numerous slender teeth
clades.notes: Kellner's broader Archaeopterodactyloidea also includes Germanodactylus; others prefer Ctenochasmatoidea/Euctenochasmatia for the lineage of Pterodactylus, gallodactylids and ctenochasmatids.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Archaeopterodactyloidea”. English Wikipedia, revision 1374260811.

clades.name: Darwinoptera (Wukongopteridae)
clades.sum: Jurassic transitional pterosaurs from China and England combining long tails with pterodactyloid-like heads and necks.
diag: Long tail and other ‘rhamphorhynchoid’ features
Long neck vertebrae
Nasoantorbital fenestra
clades.notes: Wukongopteridae was defined in 2010 (Wukongopterus + Kunpengopterus). Darwinoptera covers the same transitional lineage.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Wukongopteridae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383159371.

clades.name: Dimorphodontidae
clades.sum: Early, big-headed long-tailed pterosaurs of the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic, known from the UK and the south-western USA.
diag: Deep, lightly built skull with very large openings
Large external nostril, the largest skull opening
Fang-like front teeth followed by smaller teeth
clades.notes: Unwin's 2003 definition (Dimorphodon + Peteinosaurus) may be superfluous; Andres et al. (2014) used Dimorphodontia instead. Caelestiventus (2018) shows the group arose in the Triassic.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Dimorphodontidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383158668.

clades.name: Dsungaripteridae
clades.sum: Robust, inland pterosaurs of the Early Cretaceous with pincer-like jaw tips and crushing back teeth.
diag: Small eye socket placed high on the skull
High ridge across the snout
No teeth at the front of the jaws
Largest teeth at the back of the upper jaw
clades.notes: Commonly interpreted as eaters of hard-shelled prey. Their position (near azhdarchoids or elsewhere) is debated, so the family is placed here directly under Pterodactyloidea.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Dsungaripteridae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383158698.
Kellner, A. W. A. (2003). Pterosaur phylogeny and comments on the evolutionary history of the group. Geological Society, London, Special Publications 217: 105–137.

clades.name: Istiodactyliformes
clades.sum: Early Cretaceous pteranodontoids including the razor-toothed istiodactylids and the mimodactylids.
diag: Broad snouts
Teeth restricted to the front of the jaws; in istiodactylids triangular, compressed and interlocking
clades.notes: Istiodactylids are interpreted as scavengers. The contents of the group vary between analyses (Haopterus, Linlongopterus).

sources.text: Kellner, A. W. A. et al. (2019). First complete pterosaur from the Afro-Arabian continent: insight into pterodactyloid diversity. Scientific Reports 9: 17875. doi:10.1038/s41598-019-54042-z

clades.name: Monofenestrata
clades.sum: Pterosaurs in which the nostril and antorbital opening merged into a single large skull opening — pterodactyloids and their closest relatives.
diag: Nasoantorbital fenestra (single opening in front of the eye)
Elongated neck vertebrae
clades.notes: Named in 2010 after the discovery of Darwinopterus, which combines a pterodactyloid-type skull with a long tail. Several Jurassic forms (Douzhanopterus, Propterodactylus, Skiphosoura, Makrodactylus, Laueropterus) document the transition.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Monofenestrata”. English Wikipedia, revision 1353613677.

Lü, J.; Unwin, D. M.; Jin, X.; Liu, Y.; Ji, Q. (2010). Evidence for modular evolution in a long-tailed pterosaur with a pterodactyloid skull. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 277: 383–389. doi:10.1098/rspb.2009.1603

clades.name: Pteranodontia
clades.sum: Toothless, crested ocean soarers of the Late Cretaceous: Pteranodontidae and Nyctosauridae.
diag: Toothless jaws
Specialised head crests, larger in males
Very long, albatross-like wings
clades.notes: Restricted here to Pteranodontidae + Nyctosauridae, following Longrich, Martill & Andres (2018).

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Pteranodontia”. English Wikipedia, revision 1374690000.

Longrich, N. R.; Martill, D. M.; Andres, B. (2018). Late Maastrichtian pterosaurs from North Africa and mass extinction of Pterosauria at the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary. PLOS Biology 16(3): e2001663. doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.2001663

clades.name: Pteranodontoidea
clades.sum: The most diverse Cretaceous pterosaurs: istiodactyliforms, anhanguerians, pteranodontids and nyctosaurids.
diag: Long, narrow wings with a warped deltopectoral crest on the humerus
Early forms toothed; later pteranodontians toothless
clades.notes: Defined by Kellner (2003) as Anhanguera + Pteranodon and all descendants; Ornithocheiroidea is sometimes treated as a synonym. Largely replaced by azhdarchids late in the Cretaceous.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Pteranodontoidea”. English Wikipedia, revision 1346803405.
Kellner, A. W. A. (2003). Pterosaur phylogeny and comments on the evolutionary history of the group. Geological Society, London, Special Publications 217: 105–137.

clades.name: Pterodactyloidea
clades.sum: Short-tailed pterosaurs, from the Middle–Late Jurassic to the end of the Cretaceous — the group that includes all the giants.
diag: Short tail
Long wing metacarpals
Long neck and large head
Hindlimbs free of the wing membrane; walked well on all fours
clades.notes: The most derived forms lost their teeth; by the Late Cretaceous all known pterodactyloids were toothless. Kryptodrakon (~161 Ma) is the earliest known member.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Pterodactyloidea”. English Wikipedia, revision 1371223005.
Andres, B.; Clark, J.; Xu, X. (2014). The earliest pterodactyloid and the origin of the group. Current Biology 24(9): 1011–1016. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2014.03.030

clades.name: Pterosauria
clades.sum: Pterosaurs: the first vertebrates to evolve powered flight, living from the Late Triassic to the end of the Cretaceous (about 228–66 Ma).
diag: Wing membrane of skin, muscle and other tissues stretched from a hugely elongated fourth finger to the ankles
Pteroid — a unique wrist bone supporting the membrane in front of the arm
Hair-like pycnofibres covering body and parts of the wings, in some cases branched like down feathers
Warm-blooded, with air sacs and flow-through breathing that hollowed out the bones
clades.notes: Traditionally split into long-tailed ‘rhamphorhynchoids’ (a paraphyletic grade) and short-tailed Pterodactyloidea, linked by the transitional Monofenestrata. Adult sizes range from about 25 cm to perhaps 10–11 m in wingspan.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Pterosaur”. English Wikipedia, revision 1385601836.
Andres, B.; Clark, J.; Xu, X. (2014). The earliest pterodactyloid and the origin of the group. Current Biology 24(9): 1011–1016. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2014.03.030

clades.name: Rhamphorhynchidae
clades.sum: Long-tailed Jurassic pterosaurs named after Rhamphorhynchus — the classic ‘rhamphorhynchoids’ with tail vanes.
diag: No more than 11 pairs of teeth in the snout
Deltopectoral crest narrow at its base and expanded at the tip
Bent phalanx on the fifth toe
Rhamphorhynchines: lightly built, pointed jaws with forward-pointing (procumbent) teeth
clades.notes: Traditionally divided into Rhamphorhynchinae and Scaphognathinae; not all analyses recover both groups.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Rhamphorhynchidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383159186.
Andres, B.; Myers, T. S. (2013). Lone Star pterosaurs. Earth and Environmental Science Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 103: 383–398.

clades.name: Scaphognathidae
clades.sum: Robust, short-snouted long-tailed pterosaurs of the Jurassic, with few, widely spaced vertical teeth.
diag: Broad-tipped skull
Few, widely spaced, vertically oriented teeth
Robust skeleton and relatively short wings
clades.notes: Treated as a subfamily (Scaphognathinae) of Rhamphorhynchidae by many authors and as a separate family by others; both views place it among long-tailed breviquartossans.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Rhamphorhynchidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1383159186.

clades.name: Tapejaridae
clades.sum: Small to medium crested, toothless pterosaurs of the Cretaceous, probably of Asian origin — including the first known plant-eating pterosaurs.
diag: Bony crest arising from the snout, often supporting a larger soft-tissue crest
Very large nasoantorbital fenestra (at least half of skull length)
Small pear-shaped eye sockets
Downturned beak
clades.notes: Brain-case studies indicate excellent vision. Gut contents of Sinopterus show herbivory.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Tapejaridae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1385511302.

clades.name: Thalassodromidae
clades.sum: Large-crested azhdarchoids from the Albian Romualdo Formation of Brazil: Thalassodromeus, Tupuxuara and Kariridraco.
diag: Huge bony head crests
Toothless, blade-like jaws
clades.notes: Originally a subfamily of Tapejaridae; other analyses place it closer to azhdarchids and dsungaripterids. Placed here directly under Azhdarchoidea.

sources.text: Wikipedia contributors. “Thalassodromidae”. English Wikipedia, revision 1384648658.
